entries.narration: This is web-01, a server the Sysops team is about to set up, and the first thing worth knowing is that it has two names. Ask the file called os-release what this system is, and it answers Debian GNU Linux thirteen, trixie. Ask the command uname for the kernel's release, and it answers six point twelve point one hundred and thirteen. Both answers are true, because Linux, strictly, is only the kernel: the program that starts first and runs everything else. It decides which process gets the processor, hands out memory, reads and writes files on the disk, and talks to the network card. Everything you type reaches the hardware through it, by asking the kernel with system calls. Debian is a distribution: the kernel plus thousands of packaged programs, sensible defaults, and a way of installing and updating all of it. That is why the picture has layers. The distribution sits on the kernel, and the kernel sits on the machine, here an x eighty six sixty four virtual machine, as uname minus m reports. Distributions come in families that share the same kernel but differ in their tools and defaults. Debian and Ubuntu are one family, and this server, web-01, carries it through courses one to ten. Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Rocky and Alma are the other big family, and in the final course the team does the same job again on Rocky Linux, so that you see what changes between them and what stays the same. Every output in this course comes from really running the command on a real virtual machine. Nothing is typed by hand.

Here is what the Sysops team will build, and what you will learn along the way. On the left is ops, the team's workstation. Every session in this course starts there, and reaches the server with ssh. In the middle is web-01, the Debian server, and each card on it is one course. First the shell, finding your way around. Then packages, which is how we install the nginx web server. Then text tools, because on Linux almost everything is text: settings, logs, and the output of commands, joined together with pipes, and nginx's own log is what we read with them. Then users and permissions, because a server is shared and every file has an owner. Processes, the running programs, and how to see and stop them. Services, which keep nginx running and restart it after a reboot, with the logs that tell you what happened. The network: addresses, ports, a firewall, and a certificate so the site is served over HTTPS. Storage: disks, filesystems, and what to do when one fills up. And scripts, which turn the team's routine into one command that runs on a schedule. On the right is the result, sysops dot example, served by nginx from web-01. Below it, greyed out for now, is web-02, a Rocky Linux server, where the final course repeats the job the Red Hat way, with its own package manager, firewall and SELinux. The course has one rhythm. Each section adds one thing the server needs, teaches the part of Linux that does it, and shows the real output. Some sections break the server on purpose, so you see a failure and how to recover from it, before you meet it for real. Let's log in.

Every session starts on ops, the team's workstation, at a prompt that reads sysops at ops. Typing ssh web-01 opens a secure connection to the server, and logs in with the team's key, so no password is asked for. The server greets us with its kernel version and Debian's licence notice, and tells us when this account last logged in. Then the prompt changes, and the prompt is the first thing to read on any Linux machine. sysops is who you are, which whoami confirms. web-01 is the machine your commands now run on, which hostname confirms. This matters more than it seems: two terminals can look identical while one is your workstation and the other a production server. After the colon is where you are. The tilde is short for your home directory, and pwd, print working directory, spells it out: slash home slash sysops. The last character is the dollar sign, which means an ordinary user. Now sudo minus i. sudo runs a command as the administrator, called root, and asks for your own password first, which is not echoed as you type. The prompt now ends in a hash sign, whoami says root, and its home is slash root. As root, nothing asks you to confirm anything, so the habit is simple: become root for a task, and type exit as soon as it is done. Exit again closes the connection, and we are back on ops.

A command line has three kinds of parts, and once you can tell them apart, most commands read the same way. First, the command itself: a program to run. Here it is ls, which lists files. In the home directory it prints nothing, because the home directory is still empty of visible files. Give it an argument, slash etc slash ssh, and it lists that directory instead: the configuration of the ssh server we just logged in through. An argument says what to run the command on. Options say how to run it, and they start with a dash. Minus l asks for the long format: the permissions, the owner, the size and the date of each file. Add minus h, and the size of sshd config reads three point four K instead of a count of bytes. Short options can be combined, so minus l h means exactly the same as minus l minus h, and a command can take several arguments, here two files listed at once. Many options also have a long form with two dashes, so minus a and minus minus all are the same option. And minus a is worth knowing: names that start with a dot are hidden from a plain ls, and minus a shows them, the shell's settings and the ssh directory among them. Finally, an option a command does not know. ls minus z stops before doing anything: it names the invalid option, and points you to minus minus help. That is the next section.

Nobody remembers every option, and you are not expected to. Linux gives you two ways to look them up on the machine itself. The quick one is minus minus help, which prints a summary straight into the terminal and returns to the prompt. The full one is the manual, opened with man and the command's name. On the left is the manual page for ls, exactly as the terminal showed it. It takes over the whole screen, which is why the console disappears while you read. Every page has the same shape: the name and a one line description, a synopsis showing the order of options and arguments, then a description of every option. The square brackets in the synopsis mean optional, and the three dots mean you can repeat it. The line at the bottom is the pager, and the pager is less, so the same keys work in both: space for the next page, b to go back, slash and a word to search, and q to quit back to the prompt. The manual is split into numbered sections. man minus f, on the right, shows which sections a name appears in. ls is in section one, commands anyone can run. passwd is in section one too, the command that changes a password, and also in section five, the format of the file slash etc slash passwd. Section eight holds administration commands. When a page refers to passwd with a five in brackets, it means that file format, not the command. The manual describes the version actually installed, which a page on the web may not.

On Linux there are no drive letters. Everything lives in one tree that starts at a single directory, called root and written as one slash, and every disk, device and setting has a place somewhere under it. This is the real top of web-01's tree, from ls minus F, which marks each directory with a slash and each symbolic link with an at sign. The names are the same on almost every Linux system, so learning them once pays off everywhere. slash etc holds configuration: ssh's settings, the list of users, and later the web server's site. slash usr holds the installed programs and their libraries. On Debian thirteen, bin, sbin and lib at the top are only links into slash usr, kept so old paths still work. slash boot holds the kernel itself. slash var is for data that changes as the system runs, and the most important part of it for an administrator is slash var slash log. slash srv is for data the server serves, and it is empty for now, which is where the team's site will go. slash tmp is scratch space, cleared at boot. slash home has one directory per person, and here only sysops, while the administrator's home is slash root. The last three are not files on a disk at all. slash proc and slash sys are the kernel describing itself, the running processes and the devices, as if they were files. slash dev holds the devices, disks and terminals among them. Course six reads slash proc, and course nine works under slash dev.

A path is the route to a place in the tree, and there are two kinds. An absolute path starts with a slash, at the root, so it means the same thing wherever you are. cd, change directory, slash etc slash ssh takes us there, and the prompt now shows the new place, as pwd confirms. A relative path starts from wherever you are now. Two dots mean the directory above this one, so dot dot slash default goes up from ssh to etc, and then down into default: slash etc slash default. One dot means this directory, which you will need later, to run a program from the current folder. The tilde means your home directory, so cd tilde brings us back to slash home slash sysops, from anywhere. Relative paths work for any command, not just cd. From home, ls dot dot slash dot dot goes up twice, to the root, and lists it. And there is one shortcut worth keeping: cd minus goes back to the last place you were, and prints it. Here, from slash var slash log back to home. Two habits avoid most mistakes with paths. Read the prompt before you act, because it always says where you are. And in anything that will run later or on another machine, a script, a service, a setting, use absolute paths, because nobody can be sure where it will be started from.

Time to make something. mkdir makes a directory, site, and touch makes an empty file in it, index dot html. cp copies a file: copy dot html is a second file with the same contents, so changing one never changes the other. mv moves a file, and moving within the same directory is how Linux renames: copy dot html becomes about dot html. Nothing is copied, the file just gets a new name. One more directory, css, and one file with something in it, a copy of slash etc slash hostname called notes dot txt. Now the misconception worth catching early. mv and cp onto a name that already exists do not ask: they replace the old file, silently. With minus i, interactive, they ask first. Here mv minus i asks whether to overwrite notes dot txt, the answer is n, and cat shows the old contents are still there: web-01. Removing is where to slow down. rm about dot html removes the file immediately. There is no recycle bin and no undo. rm refuses to remove a directory on its own, with the error is a directory, and that refusal is a safety feature. To remove a directory and everything in it, rm takes minus r, recursive, and here minus i as well, so it asks before each of its five steps, ending with site itself. On a real server, rm minus r with the wrong path, or as root, is one of the classic ways to destroy a system. So the habit is to list the exact path first, read the prompt to know which machine you are on, and only then remove it. The home directory is empty again.

Most of an administrator's day is reading files, and Linux has a tool for each size of file. cat prints a whole file. It is right for short ones, like slash etc slash hostname, which holds a single line: web-01. head shows the first lines of a file and tail shows the last, with minus n for how many. slash etc slash passwd is the list of accounts, one per line. Its first lines are root and the system accounts, and its last line is ours, sysops, with its home directory and its shell. tail matters most for logs, where the newest entries are at the end. wc minus l counts lines: this file has twenty eight, one per account. For anything longer than a screen, there is less. It shows one screen at a time, and on the left is less showing a file called README, in slash var slash log. It is a real message from Debian, and an important one. On this system the traditional text log files are gone, replaced by the systemd journal, which keeps the same information and is read with a command called journalctl. Course seven uses it. less uses the keys you met in the manual: space and b to move, slash to search, and q to quit. And unlike opening a file in an editor, less can never change it, which makes it the safe way to look at anything on a server, including the settings you are about to edit.

The Sysops team needs a web server on web-01, and on Linux you almost never download a program from a website and run an installer. You ask the package manager, which on Debian is apt. It installs software from an archive: a large collection of packages that the distribution builds, tests and signs. This file, debian dot sources, tells apt where the archive is. URIs is its address. This lab uses a dated snapshot of Debian's archive, frozen in October, so every replay installs exactly the same versions. Suites names the release, trixie, plus its updates. Components main is the free software Debian supports. And Signed-By names the key that proves the lists really come from Debian, so a tampered mirror is refused. apt update downloads the archive's index, the lists of every package and version, here sixteen point eight megabytes of them. It changes nothing installed. It only refreshes what apt knows exists. Then apt-cache policy asks about one package, nginx. It is not installed yet. Two versions are on offer: one from the release itself, and a newer one from trixie-security, where Debian publishes security fixes. The newer one is the candidate, the version apt would install. The flow on the right is the whole job: the archive, the index apt update fetched, apt deciding what to install, and dpkg, the lower-level tool that unpacks the files onto the disk.

Installing changes the system, so it needs sudo. sudo apt install nginx asks for the password, then apt works out the plan before it touches anything. It will install nginx, which you asked for, and nginx-common, a dependency: the settings and the service that the nginx program needs. Three more packages are only suggested, so they are not installed. Read the summary before you answer, because it is the last moment to stop: two packages to install, nothing to remove, seven hundred and twenty five kilobytes to download, and under two megabytes of disk. The question is continue, with a capital Y, which means Enter alone answers yes. If the plan ever wants to remove packages you did not expect, answer n. The middle of the output is folded on the screen: the downloads, then dpkg unpacking each package and setting it up. Two lines at the end matter. Created symlink means the install registered nginx as a service that starts at every boot, and course seven explains what that link is. And the install also started it. curl minus capital I asks a web server for just the headers of its home page, and nginx answers straight away: two hundred OK, the server's name, and a page of six hundred and fifteen bytes. That page is nginx's welcome page, the default site, still waiting for content of its own. The team will replace it with sysops dot example later in the course.

A package is a set of files, and dpkg remembers every one it installed. dpkg minus capital L lists them. The nginx package is small: the program itself in slash usr slash sbin, its documentation, and its manual page. Going the other way, dpkg minus capital S asks which package owns a file. The main configuration, slash etc slash nginx slash nginx dot conf, belongs to nginx-common, the dependency. That split is common on Debian: settings and data in one package, the program in another. Each kind of file went where the filesystem tree says it should. Settings in slash etc slash nginx. ls minus F marks the directories, and two of them, sites-available and sites-enabled, are where the team's own site will go. The page nginx is serving is in slash var slash www slash html. And the logs are in slash var slash log slash nginx: an access log with a line for every request, and an error log. Look at their owner and mode. They belong to www-data, the account nginx runs as, and the group adm, and only the owner can write them while the group can read. sysops is in the adm group, which is why the team can read the logs without sudo. That is the next course, so keep the access log in mind. Finally, two questions to systemd. Is nginx active? Yes, it is running now. Is it enabled? Yes, it will start at every boot. A package can install a service and switch it on, and on a server that is worth checking every time.

Software keeps changing after it is installed, mostly to fix security problems, so keeping packages current is a routine job. apt-cache policy nginx again. Installed and candidate are now the same version, and the three stars mark the one on the disk. The extra line that reads one hundred, slash var slash lib slash dpkg slash status, is dpkg's own record of what is installed. Three verbs sound alike and do different things. apt update refreshes the lists of what exists, and installs nothing. apt upgrade moves the installed packages to their candidates. And apt install adds a package and whatever it needs. apt list minus minus upgradable shows what an upgrade would change, and here it shows nothing, and the upgrade agrees: zero to upgrade. That is because this archive is a frozen snapshot, and this lab has also switched off Debian's automatic security updates, so nothing can change in the middle of a recording. On a real server, the opposite is the goal. Run apt update and apt upgrade regularly, or leave it to the unattended-upgrades service, which Debian installs for exactly that. One more distinction. apt-mark showmanual lists packages installed manually, because someone asked for them, and of the two it names only nginx. nginx-common was installed automatically, as a dependency. That is what lets apt autoremove clean up later: when nothing needs an automatic package any more, it can go, while a manual one stays until you remove it yourself.

On Linux, almost everything an administrator handles is text: settings, logs, and the output of every command. The tools in this course all work on text, and they all rest on one idea. Every process starts with three open files, numbered zero, one and two. Zero is standard input, where it reads from. One is standard output, where its results go. Two is standard error, where its complaints go. By default all three lead to your terminal, and the system shows this directly: ls minus l slash proc slash self slash fd lists the open files of the ls that is running, and zero, one and two all point at slash dev slash pts slash zero, this terminal. Watch the two output streams separate. ls is asked for two files, one that exists and one that does not. On the terminal, the name and the error look the same. Add a greater-than sign and a file name, and the shell sends standard output to the file instead. The file name went into out dot txt, as cat shows, but the error still reached the screen, because it travels on the other stream. Two greater-than sends standard error alone, and now the error is in err dot txt and the result is on the screen. This is the design, not an accident. A program's results can go to a file, or into the next program, while its errors still reach the person who needs to see them. And there is one more place to send a stream: slash dev slash null, which discards whatever is written to it, as you will see in a few minutes.

Since nginx was installed, its access log has been filling up. For this course the team sent the server about a hundred real requests from a handful of test addresses, the way browsers and bots would, so the log has something to read. wc minus l counts its lines: one hundred and eight, one per request. head shows the first two. The first is the curl from the last course. The second is a typical line, and the table reads it field by field: the client's address, the time, the request itself, a GET of the home page, the status two hundred, meaning OK, the bytes sent, and the user agent, the name the client gave itself. Now the most important character on the command line, the vertical bar, called a pipe. grep keeps only the lines that contain the text you give it, here a space, four oh four, and a space: requests for pages that do not exist. On its own, grep prints them all. Piped into head, only the first three reach the screen, and they show who was asking: one address, requesting wp-login dot php, a WordPress login page this server has never had. That is a bot, probing. Piped into wc minus l instead, the lines are counted: twenty two requests got a four oh four. A pipe connects one program's standard output to the next program's standard input. grep does not know wc exists, and wc does not know where its lines came from. Each program does one small job, and the shell joins them, which is why Linux has so many small tools instead of a few large ones.

grep searches with patterns, and a pattern can say much more than plain text. Start plain. grep minus c counts matching lines instead of printing them: nine requests mention wp-login. Now three questions at once. Minus capital E turns on extended patterns, and inside round brackets a vertical bar means or: a request for wp-login dot php, or dot env, or admin. The backslash before each dot matters, because in a pattern a bare dot means any character at all, and the backslash makes it a real dot. Nineteen requests probed one of those three paths. Square brackets are a set of characters, so four or five in brackets means one character, a four or a five, and zero to nine in brackets followed by two in curly braces means exactly two digits. Together, after a quote and a space, that is any status in the four hundreds or five hundreds: a client error or a server error. Twenty two lines, and since this server has had no server errors, that matches the four oh fours from the pipe. Minus v inverts the match. Lines without the word Mozilla, which every browser puts in its user agent, are twenty eight: the requests from tools and bots. And minus o prints only the part of the line that matched, instead of the whole line. The caret anchors a pattern to the start of the line, so this one picks the client addresses in the sixties out of the log. Patterns like these are called regular expressions, and the same pieces work in many tools, editors and programming languages.

Here is a question an administrator really asks: which clients are hitting this server the most? No single tool answers it, but five small ones do, and the way to build a pipeline is one stage at a time, checking the output as you go. cut takes fields out of each line. Minus d says the fields are separated by a space, and minus f one takes the first field, the client's address. Checking with head, that works. Next, sort puts equal lines next to each other, and uniq minus c collapses each run of equal lines into one, with a count in front. That is already the answer, one line per client, and the chart draws it: forty three requests from the busiest address, then twenty five, twelve, eight, and fifteen from the bot that probed for wp-login. To rank them, sort again, minus r for reverse, minus n to compare the counts as numbers rather than as text, and head minus n three keeps the top three. The same pipeline with a different field answers a different question. Field nine is the status code, and the log holds eighty six two hundreds and twenty two four oh fours. Notice how little each tool knows. cut does not know what an IP address is, and uniq only compares a line with the one before it, which is why sort has to come first. Forgetting that sort is the classic mistake with uniq: the counts come out split and wrong, with no error to warn you.

grep searches inside files. find searches for files, walking down the tree from a starting directory and testing each entry it finds. The first test is the name. find slash etc slash nginx minus name, then a pattern in quotes, finds four files ending in dot conf, including two in the snippets directory, because find looks inside every directory below where it starts. The quotes matter, and the next section shows why: they keep the star for find to match, instead of letting the shell expand it first. Searching slash var slash log for files ending in dot log finds the logs, and one error. sysops is not allowed to read slash var slash log slash private, and find says so on standard error, in the middle of the results. That is exactly what two greater-than slash dev slash null is for: standard error goes nowhere, and the results stay clean. Use it only when you understand the error you are hiding, because it hides every error, not just this one. Other tests look at what an entry is, not what it is called. Minus type l finds symbolic links, and slash etc slash nginx has one: the link in sites-enabled that switches the default site on, which course seven comes back to. Minus size plus five M finds files bigger than five mebibytes, here four in slash usr, the largest files the system installed. The tests combine. Minus type f with minus size means regular files that are also that big.

Before any program runs, the shell rewrites the line you typed, and most surprising behaviour on the command line comes from that rewrite. echo prints whatever arguments it was given, which makes it the perfect way to see what the shell passed. A star is a glob, a pattern for file names. echo slash etc slash nginx slash star dot conf prints two real file names, because the shell matched the pattern against the directory and replaced it, before echo started. echo never saw the star. Put the same text in single quotes, and it is passed exactly as typed. And when a glob matches nothing, bash leaves it as typed, which is why a pattern that finds no files can turn into a strange argument instead of an error. A dollar sign expands a variable. HOME holds your home directory, so echo dollar HOME prints slash home slash sysops. Single quotes stop that too, and print a literal dollar HOME. Double quotes are the middle ground: they keep the text as one word, but still expand variables. Spaces are the last part. Unquoted, two words separated by five spaces arrive as two separate arguments, and echo joins them with one space. Quoted, they arrive as one argument with every space kept. That is why a file name containing a space needs quotes, and why, in scripts, every variable should be in double quotes. The order on the right is the summary: variables, then word splitting, then globs, then the quotes are removed, and only then does the program start.

Sooner or later every administrator edits a file on a server, and two editors are almost always there. nano is the friendly one. Its bottom two rows list its shortcuts, and the caret means the Control key, so Control O writes the file out and Control X exits. If you only remember one thing about nano, remember that the help is always on the screen. vim is the one installed on nearly every Unix system, including the smallest rescue environments, so it is worth knowing enough to survive in it. The thing that confuses everyone at first is that vim has modes. It starts in normal mode, where keys are commands, not text. Pressing i switches to insert mode, and vim says so on its bottom row: dash dash INSERT dash dash. On the left is vim exactly as the terminal showed it, with the team's first note typed in: web-01, nginx installed, serving the default page. The numbers on the right of the bottom row are the cursor's position, line one, column fifty one. Escape goes back to normal mode, and a colon opens the command line at the bottom. Colon w q writes the file and quits. Colon q exclamation mark quits and throws your changes away, which is the way out when you are lost. The file stays on the server for the rest of the course. Whichever editor you prefer, look at a file with less first, and keep a copy before editing anything that a service depends on.

A server is shared: by people, and by the programs that run on it. Linux keeps them apart with users and groups, and every file and process belongs to one of each. id answers who you are. sysops is user one thousand, its primary group is sysops, and it is also in a group called adm, number four. Underneath, the system only uses the numbers. The names are for people. id www-data shows a very different account: the one nginx runs as, user thirty three. getent reads the account database, and the two lines show the difference. sysops has a home in slash home and the bash shell. www-data's home is slash var slash www, and its shell is nologin, a program that refuses every login. A service gets its own account like this so that a fault in it can only reach what that account may touch, never the whole system. Groups are listed in slash etc slash group, one line per group with its members at the end. adm lists sysops, and that is why the team could read nginx's log in the last course without sudo: the log's group is adm, and adm may read it. The sudo group, by contrast, is empty. sysops can still use sudo, for a reason the fifth section shows. The passwords themselves are not in slash etc slash passwd at all. The x in the second field points to slash etc slash shadow, which holds the password hashes, and which is the next section's example of a file you are not allowed to read.

Every file carries a mode: ten characters at the start of ls minus l. The first says what it is: a dash for a file, d for a directory, l for a link. The other nine are three groups of three. The first triplet is for the file's owner, the second for its group, and the third for everyone else, and in each, r means read, w means write, and x means execute, with a dash where the permission is missing. The team's notes file is r w dash, r w dash, r dash dash. Its owner sysops and its group sysops may read and write it, and everyone else may only read it. Now slash etc slash shadow, the password hashes. Its owner root may read and write, its group shadow may read, and others may do nothing. The important rule is that Linux checks only one triplet. If you own the file, the owner's triplet applies. Otherwise, if you are in its group, the group's. Otherwise, others. sysops is neither root nor in the shadow group, so it is others, with no read permission, and cat is refused with permission denied. That error is the system working as designed, not a fault to work around. Two directories show special letters. sysops's home is r w x for its owner and nothing at all for anyone else, so other users cannot even look inside. slash tmp is writable by everyone, and ends in a t, the sticky bit: anyone may create files there, but only a file's owner may delete it.

chmod changes a mode, and there are two ways to write the change. With numbers, each triplet becomes one digit: read is four, write is two, execute is one, and the digit is their sum. So six is read and write, four is read only, and zero is nothing. chmod six zero zero makes the notes private to their owner, and ls confirms r w dash, then nothing for the others. With letters, you say who and what to change. g o plus r adds read for the group and others, and leaves everything else as it was. stat prints the mode both ways: six four four, which is r w dash, r dash dash, r dash dash. Numbers set the whole mode at once, which is what you want in a script. Letters change one thing, which is safer by hand. chown changes the owner, and that needs root. After sudo chown root, the file belongs to root, and sysops falls through to the group triplet, which is read only. Appending a line with two greater-than signs is refused: permission denied, from bash, because the shell opens the file for writing before echo even runs. Giving the file back to sysops restores the owner's read and write. Note who may do what. Anyone who owns a file may chmod it. Only root may chown it, so that users cannot give files away to someone else. Both are ordinary changes to the file's details, and both take effect for the very next access.

The same three letters mean something different on a directory, and this is where most permission puzzles come from. On a directory, r lets you list the names in it. w lets you create, rename and delete entries. And x lets you pass through it, to reach what is inside. To see the difference, a directory called box with one file in it gets mode six zero zero: read and write, but no x. ls box can read the names, so the name file appears, but ls cannot look at the file itself and complains, because getting its details means going through box. cat box slash file is refused outright: without x on box, nothing inside it can be opened, whatever the file's own mode says. With seven zero zero, x is back, and cat reads the word inside. The practical rule follows from this. To open slash srv slash sysops dot example slash index dot html, a user needs x on every directory along the way: on slash, on slash srv, and on slash srv slash sysops dot example, and then r on the file itself. One missing x anywhere on the path, and the file is out of reach. ls minus l d shows the walk to the team's notes. slash and slash home let everyone pass. notes dot txt itself may be read by others. But sysops's home is r w x for its owner only, so another user stops there, and never reaches the file. When nginx answers four oh three forbidden later in this course, that is the first thing to check, for the www-data account, along the whole path. The practice directory is removed again with rm minus r.

root, user zero, may do anything, and that is exactly why the team never logs in as root. They use sudo, which runs one command as root and records that it did. sudo minus l asks what you are allowed to do. It needs your own password first, then shows some default settings, and finally the rule that matters: sysops may run ALL commands, as any user. That rule lives in a file. The main one is slash etc slash sudoers, and extra rules go in slash etc slash sudoers dot d. This one was written by cloud-init when the server was created, which is why sysops has sudo without being in the sudo group. Read it as four parts: the user, the hosts the rule applies on, which users the commands may run as, and which commands. Rules like this are edited with visudo, never a plain editor, because visudo checks the syntax before saving, and a broken sudoers file can lock everyone out of root. Now count the password prompts. The first sudo asked. The next three did not, because sudo remembers a successful password for a while, fifteen minutes by default on Debian, per terminal. sudo minus k forgets it immediately, and the next sudo asks again. That is a good habit when you step away from a terminal. Remember too that the password sudo asks for is yours, not root's.

The team's site needs a directory that several accounts can edit: sysops, and later a deploy account that publishes the site automatically. The tool for that is a group. groupadd creates a group called site. useradd minus minus system creates deploy, an account with no password and no shell, whose primary group is site. usermod minus a capital G adds site to sysops's groups. The minus a means append, and forgetting it replaces all of sysops's other groups, a classic mistake. The directory slash srv slash sysops dot example belongs to root and the group site, with mode two seven seven five. Seven seven five gives the owner and the group everything. The leading two is setgid, which shows as an s in the group's triplet, and on a directory it means new files take the directory's group, site, instead of their creator's. Now the surprise. touch is refused, and id shows why: the running session still has the old list of groups. Group membership is read at login, so the team member logs out and back in, and now id includes site, and touch works. The last detail is umask, which removes permissions from every new file. Debian thirteen's default is zero zero two, which keeps group write, and index dot html comes out r w, r w, r, in group site. With the older default of zero two two, about dot html comes out without group write, and deploy could not update it. For a shared directory, the umask is part of the design.

A program on the disk is just a file. A process is a program running, with its own memory, its own open files, and a number, its process ID, or PID. Every command you type becomes a process, and the way it happens is the same every time. echo dollar dollar prints the PID of the shell itself. Now bash minus c runs a second bash as a child, which prints its own PID and its parent's, and the parent is exactly the shell's number from the line before. ps minus o pid, ppid, comm shows the same relationship for ps itself: ps has a new PID, and its parent is this shell. Here is what the shell did, in two steps. First, fork: the shell makes a copy of itself, a new process with a new PID, whose parent is the shell. Second, exec: the copy replaces the program it is running with ps, keeping the same PID. Meanwhile the original shell waits, and when ps exits, it prints the next prompt. The link in slash proc, PID, slash exe shows which program a process is running, here slash usr slash bin slash bash. Because every process was forked by another, processes form a tree, with PID one at the top, systemd, started directly by the kernel at boot. One practical warning: PIDs are just numbers handed out in order, and they will differ on your machine and from one run to the next. Never type a PID you saw somewhere else. Always read it from ps first.

ps lists processes, and its options decide which ones and which columns. pstree minus s shows the ancestors of this shell, and they tell the story of the login. systemd, PID one, started sshd, the ssh server, at boot. sshd started an sshd-session process for this login, which started another one with sysops's privileges, which started bash. And bash started pstree. Now nginx. ps minus capital C selects processes by command name, and there are three. One runs as root: the master process, which reads the configuration and opens port eighty, something only root may do. Its two children run as www-data, the account from the last course, and they are the ones that answer requests. Splitting the work that way is a common design for servers: the privileged part does as little as possible, and everything that touches the network runs with fewer rights. ps aux is the classic way to see everything, one row per process, and sorting by RSS, the memory actually in use, puts the largest first. The columns worth knowing are percent CPU and percent memory, RSS, STAT, the state, where S means sleeping and R running, and TIME, the processor time used so far. Counting every process gives about a hundred, on a server that is doing almost nothing. Most of them are the kernel's own threads, which ps shows in square brackets, and nearly all of them are asleep.

ps is a snapshot. top is the same information, refreshed every few seconds, and on the left is top exactly as the terminal drew it. The header is what to read first. The first line is the time, how long the server has been up, the number of users logged in, and the load average: the number of tasks wanting the processor, averaged over one, five and fifteen minutes. Load is not a percentage. On this two-CPU server, a load of two means both processors are busy, and a load that stays above the number of CPUs means work is queueing. The Tasks line counts the processes and their states, and as in ps, almost all of them are sleeping. The CPU line splits the processor's time: us is ordinary programs, sy is the kernel, and id is idle, which here is nearly all of it. The memory lines are where people most often misread top. free looks small on any healthy server, because Linux keeps file data in memory as cache, which it gives back the moment a program needs it. The number to read is avail Mem, what a new program could actually get. Below the header, one row per process, sorted by CPU. Capital M sorts by memory and capital P by CPU, k sends a signal to a process, the subject of the next section, and q quits. uptime prints the first line of top on its own, which is often all you need.

A signal is a short message to a process, delivered by the kernel, and it is how you stop, pause or nudge a program. kill minus l translates names to numbers: TERM is fifteen, KILL is nine, STOP and CONT are nineteen and eighteen, and HUP is one. The command is called kill, but it sends any signal. A sleep in the background is a safe thing to practise on. The ampersand starts it in the background, and the shell prints its job number and its PID. ps shows its state, S, sleeping. Plain kill sends TERM, which asks the process to stop, and gives it the chance to clean up first: finish writing a file, close its connections. sleep has nothing to clean up, and jobs reports it terminated. A second sleep gets STOP, and its state becomes T, stopped, and the shell notices. STOP cannot be refused or ignored, the kernel simply stops scheduling it. CONT lets it carry on, and its state is S again. Finally KILL. Like STOP, a program cannot catch it or refuse it: the kernel ends the process at once, and jobs reports it killed. So the rule is: ask first. Send TERM, give the program a moment, and only if it ignores you, send KILL, knowing that whatever it was writing may be left half done. HUP has a second meaning worth remembering for later: many server programs read it as reload your configuration.

The shell keeps its own list of the processes it started, called jobs, and a few keys move them around. sleep three hundred runs in the foreground: it owns the terminal, and you would wait five minutes for the prompt. Control Z sends it the STOP signal, the shell says stopped, and the prompt comes back. jobs lists it as job one. bg continues it in the background, as if it had been started with an ampersand. A second sleep starts in the background straight away, as job two. jobs minus l adds the PIDs, and the plus and minus mark the current and the previous job, which is what fg and bg use when you do not give a number. fg percent two brings job two to the foreground, and Control C interrupts it. Control C sends the INT signal, the polite interrupt that most programs treat like TERM. Job one is still running, until kill percent one terminates it. Percent and a number means a job, which saves you looking up the PID. Two limits are worth knowing. Jobs belong to the shell that started them, so when you log out, they are sent HUP and usually end. And nothing restarts them if they crash, or after a reboot. So jobs are for the few minutes you are at the terminal. Anything the server needs to keep running, like nginx, is a service, managed by systemd, which is course seven.

Every process carries a set of named values called environment variables, inherited from its parent, and a few of them shape everything you do. printenv shows HOME, USER and SHELL: where cd goes with no argument, who you are, and which shell you got. The most important one is PATH, a list of directories separated by colons. When you type a command name without a slash, the shell looks for it in each of those directories in order, and runs the first one it finds. That explains a surprise. Typing nginx minus v gives command not found, yet nginx is installed and running. It lives in slash usr slash sbin, which is not in sysops's PATH, because on Debian sbin directories hold administration programs and are on root's PATH instead. Running it by its full path works and prints the version, one point twenty six point three. type tells you what a name really is. ls is an alias the shell set up, adding colour. cd is a builtin, part of bash itself, because a separate program could not change the shell's own directory. A variable can be set for a single command by writing it in front, and the child sees it, while the shell afterwards does not have it at all. export puts a variable in the shell's environment, so every child from then on inherits it. That is how settings flow from a shell into the programs it starts.

Most of what ps and top show, they read from one place: slash proc. It looks like a directory of files, but nothing in it is on a disk. The kernel produces each file at the moment it is read, describing itself. Every process has a directory there, named by its PID, and dollar dollar fills in this shell's. Its status file starts with the name, bash, and the state, sleeping, because a shell waiting for you to type is asleep. Then the PID, and the parent's PID, which is the sshd-session from the process tree. Uid one thousand means it runs as sysops, and Umask is zero zero zero two, the umask from the last course, held by the process itself. Next to status are links. cwd points to the process's current directory, here the home directory, and exe, from the first section, to the program. cmdline holds the command that started it, here dash bash, the dash meaning a login shell. The system as a whole is in slash proc too. loadavg holds the three load averages from top, followed by the running and total number of tasks. meminfo holds the memory figures, and MemAvailable is exactly top's avail Mem. And uptime counts the seconds since the server booted. Tools come and go between distributions, but slash proc is the kernel's own interface, which is why it is worth knowing it is there.

A server has to come back on its own after a reboot, with everything it serves already running, so it is worth watching one happen. sudo systemctl reboot, and the connection closes. Back on ops, a small loop tries ssh every few seconds until the server answers, then logs in. Here is what happened in between. The machine's firmware found the disk and started GRUB, the boot loader, which loaded the kernel from slash boot. The kernel set up the hardware and started one program, systemd, PID one, which starts everything else. systemd works towards a goal called a target. The default is graphical dot target, which on a server without a desktop simply means multi-user dot target plus nothing more. A target is a list of units it wants, and systemctl list-dependencies shows some of them: nginx, enabled when it was installed, ssh, so the team can log in, and login prompts on the consoles. systemd starts what it can in parallel, and systemd-analyze reports how long the kernel and then userspace took. These numbers are slow because this virtual machine is emulated, and on real hardware a boot like this takes seconds. The point is the last line: nginx is active again, and nobody started it. That is what enabled means: wanted by a target, so started at every boot. A service that is running but not enabled is a classic trap, because everything looks fine until the first reboot.

systemctl is how you talk to systemd, and status is the first thing to run when a service misbehaves. Its first lines say which unit file defines nginx, and that it is enabled. Active says it is running and since when. The Process lines are worth noticing: before starting, systemd ran nginx minus t, the configuration test, so a broken configuration can never start. The CGroup is the master and its two workers, which systemd keeps together as one group, so stopping the service stops all of them. The last lines are its most recent log entries. Now stop it. is-active says inactive, and from the outside the site is simply gone: curl cannot connect at all, because nothing is listening on port eighty. No error page, no message, just a refused connection, which is worth recognising. start brings it back, and is-active agrees. The important distinction is between two separate switches. start and stop decide whether a service runs now. enable and disable decide whether it starts at boot. is-enabled confirms both nginx and ssh are enabled. Restart is stop then start, which drops every connection for a moment. Reload asks the service to re-read its configuration while it keeps serving, and nginx supports it, which is why reload is the one to use after a configuration change.

Time for the team's own site. The page goes into slash srv slash sysops dot example, the directory from course five, and a server block tells nginx about it. This is the file as the server has it. listen eighty default server means port eighty, and this site answers any request whose name no other site claims. server name is the name a browser sends in the Host header. root and index say where the files are, and that a request for slash means index dot html. access log gives the site its own log, separate from the default one the text course read. And try files returns the file, or a directory, or a four oh four. On Debian, nginx keeps every site it knows in sites-available, and serves only those linked into sites-enabled. So enabling the site is a symbolic link, made with ln minus s, and disabling the welcome page is removing its link, not its file. ls minus l in sites-enabled now shows one link, pointing at the team's file. Nothing has changed for visitors yet. nginx read its configuration when it started, and it will not notice these files until it is told to reload, which is exactly the moment to check the configuration first. That is the next section.

Changing a running server's configuration has a safe order, and this section shows why. First, nginx minus t tests the whole configuration without touching the running server. Syntax is ok, test is successful. Then systemctl reload, and nginx switches to the new configuration without dropping a single connection. curl shows the team's page, sysops dot example. Now the mistake everyone makes once. A single semicolon goes missing, after the root line. nginx minus t refuses it, and the message is precise: an invalid number of arguments in the root directive, in the team's file, at line six. Without the semicolon, nginx read root and the next line as one directive. Now suppose nobody tested, and the change was applied with restart. Restart stops the running nginx first, and only then starts the new one, which fails on the bad configuration. systemctl says the job failed, is-active says failed, and curl cannot connect. The site is down, and stays down until someone notices. reload would have been safer, because the running nginx checks a new configuration and keeps the old one if it is bad. Putting the semicolon back, nginx minus t passes, start brings the site back, and curl shows the page again. The habit is short enough to always follow: edit, nginx minus t, reload, then check from the outside with curl.

Every service's messages go to the journal, systemd's log, and journalctl reads it. This is where Debian thirteen keeps the logs that slash var slash log slash README talked about in course two. Minus u selects one unit, and nginx's history is all there: starting, started, reloading, reloaded, the stop and the start from the last section, and how much processor time each run used. Every line carries the time, the host, and who logged it. Minus p err filters by priority, showing only errors and worse, and it finds exactly one entry: failed to start nginx dot service, systemd's own record of the restart that went wrong in the last section. On a busy server, that filter is the quickest way to find the moment something broke. Underscore COMM equals sudo filters by the program that wrote the entry, and this is the record promised in course five: sudo logs every command it runs. Read one: the user, sysops, the terminal, the directory, the user it ran as, root, and the full command, here starting nginx. On a shared server, that record is how a team answers the question, who changed what. disk usage shows how much space the journal takes, a few megabytes here, and the journal rotates itself so it never fills the disk. One more option you will use often is minus f, follow, which prints new entries as they arrive, the way tail minus f follows a growing file. sysops can read the whole system journal without sudo, because it is in the adm group.

systemd does not only run big services. A small job of the team's own can be a unit too, with the same logging and control. The job: count the site's responses by status code, the pipeline from course four, and publish the result on the site. A few requests first, so the site's log has something in it, including one for a page that does not exist. The unit file goes in slash etc slash systemd slash system. Its Service section says Type oneshot, meaning a job that runs to the end and is then done, rather than a server that keeps running. User deploy runs it as the deploy account from course five, not as root. SupplementaryGroups adm lets deploy read nginx's logs, which belong to that group. ExecStart is the command, cut, sort, uniq, writing status dot txt into the site's directory. daemon-reload tells systemd to re-read its unit files, which it needs after any change. start runs the job, and status reports inactive, dead, which for a oneshot is success: it ran, it finished, and the journal lines show it starting and finishing. The output is real: five requests answered two hundred, and one four oh four. And the file belongs to deploy, in group site, thanks to the setgid directory. Nothing in this unit runs it on its own yet. It is static: something has to start it. That something is the next section.

A timer is a unit that starts another unit on a schedule. report dot timer, next to the service, has a Timer section with two lines. OnCalendar hourly means at the top of every hour. Persistent true means that if the server was off when a run was due, the run happens as soon as it boots, so a reboot never silently skips a report. The Install section says what enable should link the timer to: timers dot target, which, like multi-user, is started at boot. daemon-reload again, then enable minus minus now, which enables the timer and starts it in one step, and the created symlink is exactly that link into timers dot target. list-timers shows when it will fire next, and what it activates: report dot service. is-enabled tells the two apart. The timer is enabled. The service is static, which is correct, because nothing should start it except the timer. From now on, status dot txt on the site refreshes every hour, under the deploy account, with every run in the journal. Many servers still do jobs like this with cron, and you will meet crontab files on older systems. Timers do the same job with the same tools as every other unit: systemctl to control them, journalctl to see what happened, and list-timers to see what will happen next. That completes the services course, and the server now keeps itself running.

A server is only useful if it can be reached, so this course follows the network from the cable to the page. ip minus b r address lists the interfaces in brief. lo is the loopback, the machine talking to itself, always one two seven point zero point zero point one. enp zero s two is the network card, and its address is ten point zero point two point fifteen, slash twenty four. The slash twenty four is the size of the local network: every address starting ten point zero point two is directly reachable, without any router in between. ip route is the table that decides where each packet goes. Addresses on the local network go straight out of enp zero s two. Everything else follows the default route, via ten point zero point two point two, the gateway. ping sends a small packet that asks for an echo, and two packets out, two back, zero percent loss: the gateway is reachable. In this lab the gateway is the lab host itself, through QEMU's virtual network, which is also where the team's ops workstation lives. On a cloud server, it would be the provider's router. Where did the address come from? netplan's file, written by cloud-init, says dhcp four true: the server asks the network for an address when it starts, matched to its card by the MAC address. On a server whose address must never change, the same file would list the address explicitly.

An address gets a packet to the right machine. A port gets it to the right program. ss lists sockets, the endpoints programs open, and minus t l n means TCP, listening, with numbers instead of names. Seven sockets are waiting for connections. With sudo and minus p, ss also says which process holds each one. Port eighty is nginx, held by the master and its two workers together. Port twenty two is sshd, on IPv4 and on IPv6. And port fifty three is systemd-resolved, the local name resolver, along with fifty three fifty five, which it uses to answer name queries from neighbours on the local network. The local address column matters as much as the port. Zero point zero point zero point zero, or the two brackets for IPv6, mean every address the machine has, so another computer can connect. one two seven point zero point zero point fifty three, on lo, means loopback only, and no other machine can reach it at all. That difference is the first question to ask about any listening service: is it meant to be reachable from outside? ss minus t n, without minus l, shows established connections instead, and there is exactly one: this very ssh session, from port twenty two on web-01, to a high-numbered port on the gateway, where the team's workstation is. Every connection is a pair of addresses and ports, one on each end.

People use names, the network uses addresses, and something has to translate. The order of places to ask is written in slash etc slash nsswitch dot conf, on the hosts line. files comes first, which means slash etc slash hosts. Then myhostname, the machine's own name. Then resolve, systemd-resolved, and finally DNS. slash etc slash hosts is a plain list of addresses and names. Its header is a warning from cloud-init, which may rewrite the file, and below it are web-01's own name and localhost. getent hosts asks the system's resolver exactly the way a program would. Asked for sysops dot example, it finds nothing and exits with status two, not found. On the internet, sysops dot example would be a record in DNS, pointing at the server's public address, and every browser in the world would find it that way. This lab has no public DNS, so the team gives the name where the lookup order checks first: one line appended to slash etc slash hosts with tee minus a, under sudo, because the file belongs to root. Now getent answers one two seven point zero point zero point one. resolvectl query asks systemd-resolved directly, and it answers too, from the same file, which it marks as synthetic, meaning it did not come from a DNS server. The lesson carries over to any server: when a name does not resolve, check what each step of that order returns, starting with the first.

Now that the name resolves, curl can talk to the site the way a browser would, and minus v, verbose, shows the whole conversation. The lines starting with an asterisk are curl describing what it does: it resolved the name to one two seven point zero point zero point one, and connected to port eighty. The lines starting with a greater-than sign are the request it sent. The first line is the method, GET, the path, slash, and the protocol version. Then headers. Host names the site wanted, which is how nginx, with several sites on one address, chooses the right server block. User-Agent names the client, and that is the field the access log records at the end of each line. The lines starting with a less-than sign are the response. The status line says two hundred OK. Then the server's headers: the date, the type of content, text slash html, its length, twenty four bytes, and when the file was last modified. After an empty line comes the body, the team's page. Asking only for the status code, with minus w, turns curl into a quick test: a page that does not exist answers four oh four. A few codes are worth knowing by heart. Two hundred is OK. Three oh one means moved, go to the address in the Location header, which this course will see soon. Four oh three is forbidden, usually permissions. Four oh four is not found. And five oh two or five oh three mean that something behind the web server failed.

Every login in this course has used a key, never a password, and this section shows why, and then switches passwords off. A key pair has two halves. The private half, on ops, never leaves that machine. The public half is in authorized keys on web-01, one line per key that may log in. ssh-keygen minus l f prints a key's fingerprint, and the fingerprint of the line in authorized keys on web-01 is identical to the public key on ops: the same pair. When ops connects, it proves it holds the private half without ever sending it, which is why a stolen copy of authorized keys is useless to an attacker. Passwords are the weakness. With the key refused on purpose, ssh falls back to asking for a password, and it works. Any server reachable from the internet receives thousands of password guesses a day, so the team turns them off. The setting goes in a drop-in file, in sshd config dot d, saying PasswordAuthentication no. The name starts with ten so it is read before cloud-init's fifty file, because for sshd the first value it reads for a setting wins. sshd minus t checks the configuration, config ok, and reload applies it. The same test again is now refused: permission denied, publickey. The rule for changing sshd is strict. Keep a second session logged in while you do it, and test from a third, because a mistake here locks out exactly the people who could fix it.

A firewall decides which packets reach the server at all. Debian uses nftables, installed from the archive like any package, three of them here. The team's rules are in one file. Its input chain has policy drop, so everything inbound is refused unless a rule accepts it. Rules are read from the top, and the first match decides. Established and related accepts the replies to connections already allowed. lo accepts the machine talking to itself. ICMP is the network's own messages, like ping. Then the two services the server exists for: port twenty two for the team's ssh, and ports eighty and four four three for the site, with a counter. Anything else falls through to the last rule, which only counts what the policy drops. nft minus c checks the file without applying it, ruleset ok. Copied to slash etc slash nftables dot conf and enabled, it applies now and at every boot. The site still answers two hundred, and the counter is still zero, because a request from the server itself arrives on lo. Now the branch the team runs only to learn from, and then throws away. insert puts a rule at the top of the chain, here a drop for port twenty two, above the accept. The session froze in the middle of typing. Tilde dot, ssh's escape, closes it, and a new login times out. There is no way back over the network. The way back is a console that does not use it, on a cloud server the provider's. So test firewall changes with a second way in, and never on a Friday evening.

Plain HTTP sends everything in the clear, so the site needs HTTPS, and HTTPS needs a certificate from an authority that browsers trust. certbot, installed from the archive with its nginx plugin, does the whole job with the ACME protocol. It asks the authority for a certificate for sysops dot example. The authority answers with a challenge: put this token at a known path on that site. certbot puts it there, the authority fetches it over port eighty from outside, which is why the firewall had to let eighty through, and having proved the team controls the site, it issues the certificate. The authority in this lab is the lab's own: Pebble, the test server Let's Encrypt publishes, running on the lab host under the name acme dot ops. It speaks exactly the same protocol, so every command here is what you would run against Let's Encrypt, apart from the server address. Its certificates are trusted only inside this lab, and they last five years, where Let's Encrypt's last ninety days. certbot saved the certificate and its key under slash etc slash letsencrypt slash live, then edited the site's server block, marking each line managed by certbot: listen four four three ssl, and the two file paths. Because of minus minus redirect, plain HTTP now answers three oh one, moved permanently, with a Location header pointing at the HTTPS address. curl over HTTPS answers two hundred. certbot also installed a timer that renews certificates before they expire, the same mechanism as the team's report timer.

Here is the whole course in one request, made the way a visitor would make it: from outside the server, from ops. On ops, sysops dot example resolves to the lab's forward to web-01, which stands in for a public address. curl connects to port four four three. On the way in, the packet meets web-01's firewall. It is a new connection, not loopback, so it falls through to the rule for the site, and the rule's counter, read afterwards over ssh, has counted it. Then TLS. curl and nginx agree on TLS one point three, nginx presents its certificate, issued for sysops dot example by the Pebble intermediate, and curl checks it: the name matches, the date is valid, and the issuer leads to a root it trusts. Only then does the HTTP request travel, encrypted: GET slash, Host sysops dot example. nginx picks the server block by that Host, maps slash to index dot html under the root directory, reads the file, and answers two hundred OK. And it records the request in the site's access log, where the client address is ten point zero point two point two: the gateway, because that is where the request came from as far as web-01 can see. Every one of those steps was a separate course: names, ports, the firewall, certificates, the site's configuration, permissions on the file, and the logs that prove it all happened. When a site does not answer, this is the list to walk through, one step at a time, from the top.

The team wants backups and other bulky data off the system disk, so web-01 has been given a second disk. lsblk lists the block devices, the things that store data in blocks. vda is the system disk, eight gigabytes, and its partitions: vda one holds the root filesystem mounted on slash, vda fifteen is the small EFI partition the firmware boots from, and vda fourteen is a tiny one the boot loader uses. vdb is the new disk, two gigabytes, with nothing on it. sr zero is this lab's cloud-init CD. Turning an empty disk into somewhere files can live takes three layers. First a partition table, which divides the disk into partitions. sfdisk minus l shows vdb has none, and a single line of input, type equals linux, gives it one partition across the whole disk, vdb one. Second, a filesystem: the structure that turns raw blocks into files and directories with names, owners and modes. mkfs dot ext four creates one, with the label data. This erases whatever was on the partition, so it is the command to read twice, checking the device name. lsblk minus f then shows each filesystem's type, label and UUID, a unique ID written into the filesystem itself. Device names like vdb follow the order disks were detected, and can change if a disk is added or removed. The UUID stays with the filesystem, which is why the next section uses it. The third layer, a place in the tree, is mounting.

A filesystem is used by mounting it on a directory, which then shows the filesystem's contents. mount slash dev slash vdb one on slash srv slash data, and findmnt confirms it. df minus h now shows two filesystems, the root and the new one, each with its own size and free space, joined into one tree. A mount made by hand lasts only until the next reboot. To make it permanent it goes in slash etc slash fstab, one line per filesystem. blkid reads the UUID, and the line names the filesystem by that UUID, then the mount point, the type, the options, and two numbers for old backup tools and the order of checks at boot. The option to notice is nofail. It tells the boot to carry on if this disk is missing. Then test the line before any reboot: unmount, and mount minus a, which mounts everything in fstab that is not yet mounted. It works, and mount adds a hint that systemd still holds the old version of the file, which systemctl daemon-reload would refresh. Now the branch the team ran to see why the test matters, and then discarded. The UUID was changed to one that does not exist, and nofail removed. After a reboot, ssh fails: the connection is reset before it can even begin. The server's own console, the screen a cloud provider lets you see, explains: the boot waited for a disk that never appeared and stopped in emergency mode, before starting ssh. And because root has no password, not even that console lets anyone log in. The fix from there is a rescue system. The prevention is nofail and mount minus a.

A full disk is one of the most common incidents an administrator meets, and it is worth practising once on purpose. This is another branch, run on the data disk and then thrown away, so the server never actually ran out. dd copies data, and copying zeros into a file with no size limit keeps going until it fails: no space left on device. The incident is what happens next, to everything else. Any program that tries to write, here tee writing a short note, gets the same error, and on a real server that program would be a database, the web server's log, or the package manager. Working an incident like this has a fixed order. The symptom is the error. df minus h answers where: which filesystem is full, here slash srv slash data at one hundred percent. du answers what: how much each directory under it holds, and du minus s h with a star makes the culprit obvious, the tmp directory, two gigabytes. Then the fix: remove what should not be there, and df confirms the space is back. On a real server, the usual culprits are logs nobody rotates, the subject of the next section, caches, and old backups. And one trap to remember: a file that was deleted while a program still has it open keeps using its space. df counts it, du cannot see it, because it no longer has a name. Restarting that program releases the space.

Logs grow forever unless something rotates them: closes the current file, renames it, starts a fresh one, and eventually deletes the oldest. On Debian that tool is logrotate, and nginx installed its rule for it in slash etc slash logrotate dot d. Read it line by line. The pattern covers every dot log file in nginx's directory. daily rotates them once a day. rotate fourteen keeps fourteen old files. compress gzips the old ones, and delaycompress waits one cycle, so yesterday's file stays readable as plain text. create says the fresh log is mode six four zero, owned by www-data and group adm, exactly what the course has been reading. And postrotate tells nginx to reopen its files, because a program writing to a renamed file would keep writing to the old one. Now the surprise. Forcing a rotation fails: logrotate is not installed. Debian thirteen's cloud image leaves it out, so this server would have kept growing its logs until the disk filled, which is the incident from the last section arriving slowly. A rule without its program does nothing, with no error anywhere. Installing it, then forcing a rotation, does the job. ls minus l shows each log renamed to dot one, and a fresh, empty file in its place, with the mode and owner from create. The site's own log keeps its old owner, root, because create applies only to the new file. logrotate's timer will now run every day.

A file on Linux is two things, and links make the difference visible. The data and its details, the owner, the mode, the size and where the blocks are, live in an inode, a numbered record in the filesystem. A name is only an entry in a directory, pointing to an inode. ls minus i shows the inode number of notes dot txt. ln makes a hard link: a second name for the same inode. ls minus l i shows both names with the same inode number, and the link count, the number after the mode, is now two. ln minus s makes a symbolic link instead, a tiny file of its own, which stores a name, the arrow in ls, notes dot txt. Now remove the original name. The hard link still reads the note, because rm removes a name, and the data stays as long as any name points to it. The symbolic link breaks: cat says no such file, because the name it stored is gone, and ls still shows it pointing at nothing, a dangling link. Moving the hard link back to the original name brings the symbolic link back to life, because all it ever had was the name. The team has already used symbolic links twice: sites-enabled in nginx, and the links systemctl enable creates. Both are switches by name, which is exactly what a symbolic link is good for. Hard links are rarer, and they only work within one filesystem, because an inode number means something only on its own filesystem.

Two tools cover most backups, and they answer different questions. tar makes an archive, one file holding a directory tree at a moment in time. minus c creates, z compresses with gzip, and f names the file, and minus capital C changes into slash srv first, so the archive holds sysops dot example and not the whole path. tar minus t lists it, and minus v shows that it kept each file's mode, owner and group, which a restore needs. An archive is what you keep for history, or send somewhere else. rsync keeps a copy identical to the source. The trailing slashes mean the contents of the directory. minus a keeps modes, owners and times. minus minus delete removes files from the copy that are gone from the source, which makes it a mirror rather than a pile. itemize changes says what it did, and on the first run every file is new. Then the team edits the page and runs it again, and rsync copies one file, index dot html, because it compares size and modification time and sends only what changed. That is what makes it the right tool for large directories and repeated runs. One honest note about these copies. Both are on the same server, on a second disk, which protects against deleting a file by mistake, but not against losing the server. A backup counts when it is somewhere else, and when someone has tried restoring from it. The team's next course automates the copy.

Anything the team types more than twice is worth writing down as a script: a file of commands the shell runs in order. site-check is five lines. The first line, hash bang slash bin slash bash, is the shebang: it tells the kernel which program should run this file. Then a comment. Then curl asks the site for its status code, and the dollar and round brackets keep what curl printed in a variable called code. echo reports it. And the last line is a test, the square brackets, comparing code with two hundred. Running it fails at once: permission denied. A new file is just text, and ls minus l shows why: no x anywhere in its mode. chmod plus x makes it executable, and dot slash runs it from the current directory, which is not on the PATH. It answers two hundred. Every command ends with an exit status, a number, and dollar question mark prints the last one. Zero means success. Anything else means failure. A script's status is that of its last command, here the test. With nginx stopped, curl gets no answer at all, so the code is three zeros, the test fails, and the status is one. The double ampersand runs the next command only after a success, and the double bar only after a failure, so site-check and-and echo up or-or echo DOWN prints DOWN. With nginx started again, it prints up. Exit status is the one convention every script, service and monitoring tool on Linux relies on.

A script becomes reusable when it takes arguments. count-status counts the requests that got one status code. Dollar one is the first argument given to the script, and the variable code holds it. The log is dollar two, the second argument, but written with a colon and a dash it gets a default: if no second argument was given, the site's rotated log is used. Then echo prints the code and, inside dollar round brackets, the result of grep minus c, counting matching lines. Every variable is in double quotes. Run with two hundred, it counts twelve requests, and with four oh four, two. Given a second argument, it reads that file instead, and counts eighty six in the original access log, the number the text course found with its pipeline. Now the most important quoting rule for scripts. args prints how many arguments it got, dollar hash, then loops over them twice. Called with two words in quotes, and three, it gets two arguments, and the first is two words, with the space inside it. The loop over dollar at in double quotes sees exactly those two. The same loop without quotes sees three, because the shell splits the unquoted words again at the space. In a script that handles file names, that difference is a file called two words being treated as two files that do not exist, or worse, two that do. So the habit is simple: quote every variable, and loop over quoted dollar at.

Three constructs cover most of what scripts decide. check-paths asks the site for several paths, and says what it found for each. for path in, followed by a list, runs the body once for each item, with path set to it. Inside, curl gets the status code for that path. case compares the code with patterns: two hundred is ok, four oh four is missing, and the star catches everything else, which counts as an error and adds one to a counter with dollar double brackets, the shell's arithmetic. After the loop, if tests whether the counter is greater than zero. If it is, the script says how many failed and exits with one. Otherwise it reports that all paths answered, and ends with success. With nginx running, three paths answer ok, the missing page is missing, which is expected, and the status is zero. With nginx stopped, every path gets three zeros, every one is an error, four paths failed, and the status is one. Notice what this script got right: a missing page is a normal answer, but no answer at all is a failure, so the exit status says something that a person or another program can rely on. That is the whole difference between a script that prints things and a check that can be trusted to run without anyone watching it.

By default, bash keeps going after a command fails, and that is the single most dangerous thing about shell scripts. publish-loose and publish-strict contain the same three steps, and all three are broken: cp copies a file that does not exist, grep reads a file that does not exist, and the last line uses a variable that was never set. publish-loose runs every line. cp fails and prints an error, then the script carries on and announces that it copied the page. grep fails, but its output goes through a pipe into wc, and a pipeline's status is that of its last command, so nobody notices. The variable is empty, so it reports deployed, followed by nothing. And the exit status is zero: success. Imagine the next line had been rm minus r on that empty variable plus a slash. publish-strict starts with set minus e u o pipefail and stops at the very first failure, with status one. Each option does one job, and the last four commands show them alone. A pipe of false into true reports zero; with pipefail it reports one, the failure inside it. An unset variable expands to nothing; with minus u, bash refuses: unbound variable. And minus e stops the script at the first command that fails.
