Put that line at the top of every script that changes anything, and read its errors as a gift, because the alternative is a script that silently does half a job.

Now the team's real script. Changes to the site are made in a staging copy, slash srv slash data slash staging, and a script publishes them. The staging directory belongs to the site group, so the team can edit it. The team copies the live page in, and adds a line. deploy-site goes in slash usr slash local slash bin, the place for programs installed by hand rather than by packages, with install minus m seven five five, which copies and sets the mode in one step. Read it from the top. set minus e u o pipefail first. Then cd slash, because sudo minus u keeps the directory you ran it from, and the deploy account may not read sysops's home. A script should never depend on where it was started. Then rsync from staging to the live directory, minus minus delete so that pages removed from staging disappear, and excluding status dot txt, which belongs to the report timer. The options are minus r l t rather than minus a, because deploy may write the files but not change owners, or set the times of a directory that root owns. Finally curl checks the site, and if it does not answer two hundred, the script says so on standard error and fails. Run as deploy with sudo minus u, rsync reports the two files that changed, and the script reports that the site answers. curl shows the new line, and ls shows the files now belong to deploy, in group site.

Two last habits turn a script into something a team can depend on. The first is shellcheck, a program that reads shell scripts and points out the mistakes people make in them. cleanup-old is a first draft written in a hurry, six lines, and shellcheck finds five problems. cd with an unquoted variable, and no plan if cd fails, which, combined with the rm below it, would delete matching files in whatever directory the script happened to be in. Looping over the output of ls, which breaks on file names with spaces. A glob that could turn a file name starting with a dash into an option. And rm of an unquoted variable. Each finding has a code you can look up, and most come with the corrected line. On deploy-site, shellcheck has nothing to say: clean. The second habit is scheduling, with the same tools as the report timer in course seven. site-check is installed in slash usr slash local slash bin, and a service runs it as deploy, with a timer that fires every five minutes: OnCalendar star colon zero slash five. Enabled and started, list-timers shows the next run less than a minute away, and starting the service by hand shows what every run will do: the journal holds site-check's own message, sysops dot example answered two hundred, followed by systemd's record that the run finished. If the site ever stops answering, the service fails, and that failure is in the journal at error priority, exactly where course seven showed how to find it.

The Sysops team has a second server to run, web-02, and this one is from the other big family. ssh lands at a different prompt: the user, host and directory are in square brackets, the Red Hat style. os-release says Rocky Linux ten point two, Red Quartz, a rebuild of Red Hat Enterprise Linux, and the commands it accepts in this course would run the same on RHEL, AlmaLinux, or, with small differences, Fedora. The kernel is six point twelve too, the same line as Debian's, built by a different team. id shows two more differences straight away. sysops gets administrator rights through a group called wheel, the Red Hat convention, rather than through a sudoers rule of its own. And id prints a context, with words like unconfined underscore u: that is SELinux, which labels every process and file, and which will matter a great deal by the end of this course. rpm minus q asks the package database about nginx, and it is not installed. Its configuration directory does not exist. Everything the team learned still applies here: the shell, the file tree, users, processes, systemd, the network and the scripts. What changes is a list of names and defaults, which the table on the right sets side by side, and this course works through it in order: packages, the firewall, and SELinux.

On the Red Hat family, the package manager is dnf, the packages are rpm files, and rpm is the lower-level tool, as dpkg is on Debian. dnf repolist lists where the packages come from. Rocky has three repositories: BaseOS, the core of the operating system, AppStream, applications such as nginx, and Extras. dnf info shows that nginx is available. The first time a user runs dnf, it downloads the repositories' metadata, and the screen shows those transfers. Then sudo dnf install. dnf prints its plan as a table, every package with its architecture, version, and the repository it comes from: nginx, and three dependencies. With minus y it does not ask, so the plan is worth reading in advance with minus minus assumeno. The first install from a repository also imports Rocky's signing key, which dnf prints in full: the same idea as Signed-By in Debian's sources file. rpm minus q l lists the files a package installed, like dpkg minus capital L. Now the difference that catches Debian administrators every time. is-enabled says disabled. On Debian, installing nginx started it and enabled it at boot. On the Red Hat family, a package installs a service and leaves it off, on the principle that nothing should start listening on a network port until an administrator decides it should. systemctl enable minus minus now does both in one step, and nginx answers. Its Server header even includes the version, where Debian's left it out.

Before touching the firewall, the team checks from outside. curl from ops gets two hundred: nginx is reachable, because this cloud image has no firewall running at all. Rocky's usual front end is firewalld, and here it is not even installed. Installing it holds a surprise: dnf adds a new kernel to the plan. firewalld needs kernel modules that this cloud image's kernel leaves out, so dnf installs a newer kernel package with them, to be used from the next reboot. On real hardware that takes seconds. In this emulated lab, building the new kernel's start-up image took about half an hour, which is one more reason to read a dnf plan before answering yes. enable minus minus now starts firewalld, and it works in zones: the network card is in the zone called public, and the public zone allows a short list of services by name. ssh is among them, which is why the session survives. http is not, so curl from ops now gets nothing back at all. Adding http and https with minus minus permanent writes the change for the next boot, and minus minus reload applies it now. A permanent change without a reload, or a reload without permanent, is the classic firewalld mistake: one of them is lost. list-services confirms, and curl from ops answers two hundred again. Underneath, firewalld writes nftables rules, and nft shows the rule for ports eighty and four four three: the same machinery as course eight, managed for you.

Now the team's own site, set up exactly the way they work on Debian. A directory in slash srv, the page written in the home directory and moved into place with mv, and a server block in conf dot d, which is where Rocky's nginx reads sites from, with no sites-enabled links. nginx minus t is happy, reload succeeds. And curl gets four oh three, forbidden. The team works through the checks that course five taught them. namei minus l walks the whole path and shows each step's mode: slash, srv and the site directory are all readable and enterable by others, and the file is readable by others. rwx says nginx may read it. The configuration is valid. nginx's own error log is the most precise of all: open of the file failed, thirteen, permission denied. That is the kernel refusing nginx, not nginx refusing a visitor. When every permission check says yes and the kernel still says no, on a Red Hat family server there is one more check, and it is the one this course has been pointing at since the first id. Every process and every file on web-02 carries a label, and SELinux decides by those labels, after the ordinary permissions have already said yes. The next section reads them.

SELinux adds a second check to every access, and both checks must pass. getenforce says Enforcing: SELinux is active and refusing what its policy does not allow. ps minus capital Z shows a process's label, and nginx runs in the domain httpd underscore t, the type for web servers. ls minus capital Z shows a file's label, and the team's page is labelled user underscore home underscore t: the type for files in home directories. The policy says a web server may not read files from people's home directories, which is exactly the protection you want if nginx were ever tricked into serving them. The page did not stay in the home directory, but it kept the label it was born with. The directory itself is labelled var underscore t, a generic type that the web server may not read either. For comparison, the default web root, slash usr slash share slash nginx slash html, carries httpd underscore sys underscore content underscore t, the type nginx is allowed to serve. The audit log records every refusal. ausearch, in its plain-text format, finds the one from the four oh three: at nine forty three, nginx unsuccessfully accessed a MAC policy controlled object, MAC meaning mandatory access control, SELinux. The raw audit record behind that sentence names the process's label and the file's label, which is everything needed to fix it. There are two wrong fixes worth naming so that you never reach for them: setting SELinux to permissive, or disabling it. Both switch the guard off for every service on the machine, to fix one file.

The right fix has two steps: change the rule for the path, then apply the rule to the files. SELinux keeps a list of path patterns and the label each should have. semanage, from the policycoreutils python package, adds one: everything under slash srv slash sysops dot example is httpd sys content t. restorecon minus R v then relabels the files to match the rules, and with minus v it says what it changed. The directory went from var t to httpd sys content t, and the page from user home t to the same. ls minus capital Z confirms, and curl now gets the team's page: sysops dot example on web-02. semanage fcontext minus l minus capital C lists the local rules added on this machine, and the new one is there. It explains why mv caused all this. A move keeps the file, label and all, so a file created in a home directory keeps the home directory's type. A copy would have taken the target directory's type, here var t, which is still wrong for a directory under slash srv. And why the rule rather than a quicker fix? chcon can set a label directly, but the next full relabel, which administrators run after policy changes, resets files to their rules, and the site would break again months later. The rule is what lasts. On Red Hat family servers, this is the most common reason for a four oh three, and now it is a two-command fix.

The course ends where it started, with checks. web-02 answers the same questions web-01 answered at the end of course ten. The system is Rocky Linux ten point two. nginx is enabled, and so is firewalld. The firewall allows http and https, as nftables did by hand on Debian. SELinux is enforcing. And the page answers. The table puts both servers side by side, every Debian value read from web-01's own transcripts. Most of what you learned did not change between the two: the kernel, the shell, the file tree, users and permissions, processes and signals, systemd and the journal, ssh, nginx, and the scripts. What changed is a list of names and defaults: apt and dnf, sites-enabled and conf dot d, a firewall written by hand and one managed by zones, and a second guard, SELinux, that Debian leaves to AppArmor. Over eleven courses, the Sysops team took a fresh virtual machine to a server that serves its site over HTTPS, behind a firewall, with logs that rotate, a backup and a mirror, a deploy script, and checks that run on their own, then did the core of it again on the other family. Every command in the course really ran, on real machines, and its output is what you saw. Running them yourself, on a machine of your own, is the step that turns having seen it into having done it.
